content: Overhead transparencies are advantageous because they are readily available, simple to set up, and less prone to mechanical failure. They do not require a projectionist, and the presenter can write directly on the film using a marking pen. Information can be dynamically built up by either drawing directly on the transparency or by adding transparent overlays. Additionally, the use of color is straightforward. However, overhead transparencies have several disadvantages. They are not suitable for large audiences, as the projected image lacks the sharpness of a slide. The projector cannot be placed in a projection booth, and if the transparencies are not carefully revised and well-presented, they may appear hastily prepared. Handwriting on transparencies does not produce an elegant result and can give the impression of last-minute preparation. This may be more acceptable if the writing or drawing is done during the presentation itself. A photocopy machine can create high-quality transparencies from printed word processor outputs, but only special transparency sheets designed for photocopying should be used. Similarly, computer printers can print directly onto special transparency sheets compatible with laser jet or color inkjet printers. It is important to note that transparencies require longer drying times than regular paper. Some computer software allows for printing transparencies as flipped documents, where text and images are reversed. These flipped transparencies are projected face down, enabling the presenter to write on the back during the presentation and later erase the writing without damaging the original. Computer-assisted presentations use the same software that produces 35-mm slides to create a screen show of slides, which can be manually or automatically timed. These slide shows can be projected directly to the audience. Notebook computers often have ports for connecting to external monitors or special projectors. While the equipment is expensive, it allows for elegant presentations, including moving text and images. However, overusing animation features can distract the audience and become irritating. A good presentation is often a simple one. Slides can be easily sorted and rearranged, and this technology is rapidly becoming the standard for visual aids. Before preparing a computer-assisted presentation, it is essential to confirm the availability of the necessary equipment. Since new technology is prone to equipment failure, having a backup of slides or overhead transparencies is advisable. It is also unwise to use new technology for the first time in an important meeting, especially in settings unfamiliar with it. Rehearsal is critical to ensure the presentation fits within the allotted time. Even experienced speakers rehearse their presentations, either alone or with colleagues. A reasonable speaking rate is no more than 120 words per minute. A word processor can provide an exact word count, and a double-spaced typed page typically contains about 240 words. For a ten-minute presentation, plan for no more than five double-spaced pages of text. A general rule is one slide per minute if the slide contains information, or one slide every 5–10 seconds if it contains only titles or key points. Skipping slides during the presentation due to an excessive number indicates poor preparation. The speaker's challenge is to maintain the audience's attention. Preparation includes checking the presentation room in advance, ensuring the podium has a microphone, remote control for slides, a pointer, and appropriate lighting. Slides should be properly arranged and provided to the technician. Speaking well requires practice, observing skilled speakers, and learning from mistakes. Enthusiasm and eagerness to share can engage the audience. If using a microphone, attach it to a stable part of clothing, such as a lapel, to avoid distracting background noise. Maintain eye contact with the audience and avoid reading directly from a script. If reading is necessary, the script should be written for listening, not reading. Prompter cards or slides can help deliver the presentation without reading. Varying tone, pitch, and volume helps sustain audience attention. Slides should be marked and numbered to avoid projection errors. International conventions recommend placing a spot in the lower left-hand corner of the slide as viewed by the naked eye, which should appear in the upper right corner when inserted. Slides should be checked before the presentation, ideally in a preview room. Be prepared for equipment failure and start the presentation with the lights on. Use filler slides if needed to avoid frequent light changes, but conclude with the lights on for a strong finish. Do not read the slides verbatim, as the audience is literate. Exceptions can be made for simultaneous translation, but providing translators with a copy of the text is preferable. Avoid going back to previous slides; instead, insert duplicates if necessary. Dual projection with two screens is useful only for side-by-side comparisons, and text slides should not be shown simultaneously. Exceeding the allotted time is considered poor manners and reflects inadequate preparation. Answer questions politely and knowledgeably, and do not dismiss or confront the questioner. Admitting I do not know is an acceptable response. To give a bad presentation, one might forget they agreed to speak or arrive late. Lack of preparation is another strategy, though it risks unintended inspiration. Preparing for the wrong audience or creating an overly complicated presentation can also ensure failure. A presentation of the wrong length, particularly one that is too long, will depress the audience. Ignoring the assigned topic or submitting a dull curriculum vitae in advance can further detract from the presentation. Poor slides with excessive information, small text, and incorrect order enhance the negative experience. A truly bad presentation is boring, with no connection between the speaker's words and the slides. Avoid looking at the audience, mumble, and read from a script with long, complex sentences. A bad presentation rarely elicits questions, as the audience simply wants to leave. If questions arise, avoid answering them directly and instead provide lengthy, irrelevant responses.
